title: Role of prior austenite grain boundary and retained austenite in strain localization of medium-carbon high-strength steels
abstract:
Exploring the micromechanical behavior of lath-martensitic quenching and tempering (Q&T), as well as quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels presents a significant challenge due to their complex multi-phase constituents and hierarchical structures. This study conducts a comprehensive comparative analysis using medium-carbon Q&T and Q&P steels with identical chemical compositions. Atom probe tomography (APT) was used to investigate the distribution of chemical elements, while high-resolution digital image correlation (HR-DIC) provided insights into nanoscopic strain localization and partitioning. Both Q&T and Q&P steels exhibit significant strain localization at prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs) due to substantial carbon segregation. Strain localization in Q&T steel at PAGBs and packet boundaries strongly depends on preferred geometric orientations, with boundaries inclined 45
                        °
                      to the loading direction experiencing severe deformation. Conversely, in Q&P steel, PAGBs adjacent to large clusters of fine lath martensite, lacking a packet with a longitudinal direction parallel to boundaries and a feasible in-lath slip system, primarily undergo deformation. Carbon partitioning from martensite to retained austenite (RA), along with coexisting carbon and manganese segregation at phase interfaces, stabilizes the RA, resulting in a neighborhood-dependent deformation behavior of RA. The existence of RA not only absorbs carbon, maintaining low strength and high deformability, but also uniformly distributes and induces stable interfaces to hinder the formation of large packets with easily activated in-lath slip transmission.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs:
Quenching and tempering (Q&T), as well as quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels, stand out as noteworthy members of advanced high-strength steels (AHSSs), garnering attention for their combination of cost efficiency and enhanced properties  [1–4] . Conventional Q&T steels achieve a commendable balance between strength and toughness due to the static recovery of dislocation and release of residual stress  [2,5] . In medium-carbon steels, at tempering temperatures ranging from low to intermediate, carbon exhibits mobility while the diffusivity of substitutional elements is too slow to significantly affect the lath martensite microstructure  [6] . Consequently, carbon predominantly governs the chemical and structural transformations, facilitating the replacement of transition carbides with cementite  [1] . However, the inherently limited deformability of carbon-saturated martensite and the presence of numerous carbide precipitates are detrimental to the ductility  [7–9] . To address this strength-ductility trade-off, a novel thermal processing route, known as the Q&P process involving a two-step heat treatment, was proposed  [3] . In the Q&P process, the steel is initially quenched to a temperature between the martensite-start ( 
                         
                            
                               M 
                            
                            
                               S 
                            
                         
                      ) and martensite-finish ( 
                         
                            
                               M

                      ) temperature range, resulting in a mixture of phases comprising both martensite and austenite. This is followed by a partitioning treatment, typically conducted at or above the quenched temperature. During the partitioning process, carbon atoms diffuse from the carbon-supersaturated martensite into the untransformed austenite, thus stabilizing the austenite at ambient temperature  [10–14] . Upon straining, the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect arises from the diffusionless shear transformation of retained austenite (RA) to martensite, providing additional strain hardening capacity and improving ductility  [15–17] .

In multiphase AHSSs including Q&P steels, the bulk deformation behavior and mechanical properties are strongly influenced by the volume fraction, morphology, and spatial distribution of individual phases  [18] . Strain partitioning between phases during plastic deformation is greatly affected by the differing strengths of the individual microconstituents  [19] . A mesoscopic strain probing method, digital image correlation (DIC), based on intrinsic microstructural features from etched surfaces, was employed to investigate heterogeneous deformation in lath-martensitic Q&P steels  [20,21] . It was reported that the deformation followed network-like plastic shear bands interconnected at high strain spots, while grains with laths parallel to the loading axis acted as effective barriers to their propagation  [20] . However, this mesoscopic resolution presents challenges in demonstrating the role of microscopic or even nanoscopic features such as phase boundaries and nano-islands of RA in local heterogeneous mechanical responses. More recently, high-resolution digital image correlation (HR-DIC), utilizing uniformly distributed nanoparticles such as non-crystalline SiO 2 , was employed to investigate strain localization and partitioning in ferrite-containing Q&P steels  [22,23] . The ferrite phase significantly accommodated externally induced strain, serving as the primary source of ductility, while pronounced strain partitioning at the ferrite/martensite interface favored micro cracks nucleation  [22] . The TRIP effect exhibited a neighborhood-dependent behavior, with RA in tempered martensite experiencing the highest amount of strain compared to RA in ferrite and RA adjacent to fresh martensite  [23] . In another study on a lamellar RA and martensite dual-phase medium-manganese steel, colonies of lamellar RA islands inclined at 45 
                         ° 
                       to the loading axis were found to experience maximum geometrical shear and accommodate the highest local strains  [24] . Despite the understanding that lamellar morphology including lath martensite size, geometric orientation, and RA distribution, plays pivotal roles in governing local responses, the lack of sufficient nanoscopic studies on strain partitioning and damage initiation continues to pose great challenges for the further application of medium-carbon, low-alloyed lath-martensitic Q&P steels. Additionally, although extensive research has explored RA stability in relation to carbon partitioning pathways  [25–28] , these analyses typically consider the overall microstructural constituents rather than concentrating on localized mechanical responses. Therefore, a more quantitative and statistical investigation on a nanoscopic scale, yet encompassing a large field-of-view, is essential to better elucidate the connection between element distribution and heterogeneous mechanical behavior.

Wang et al. conducted an in-situ HR-DIC experiment using a lath-martensitic Q&P steel, shedding light on the influence of microstructural heterogeneity primarily attributed to the lath martensite size, on strain partitioning and damage behavior  [29] . However, the small field-of-view and absence of crystallographic analysis limited the clarification regarding the critical origins of heterogeneous deformation within the lath-martensitic matrix, including packet boundaries, block boundaries, fine lath interfaces, and in-lath slip activation  [29,30] . Furthermore, the impact of RA on lath martensite deformation, along with the substantial interactions at the numerous RA/martensite interfaces, has not been adequately addressed in a directly comparative and quantitative manner. In the hierarchical structure of lath-martensitic Q&T and Q&P steels, the prior austenite grain is considered a pivotal factor governing mechanical properties  [31] . Observations regarding strain localization at prior austenite grain boundary (PAGB) in Q&T steel have varied; while some studies did not observe specific strain localization and attributed it to the curvature of these boundaries not favoring interface plasticity  [30] , others have reported severe strain localization at PAGBs with similar lath martensite microstructures by analyzing more prior austenite grains  [32] . This discrepancy may stem from differences in composition and thermomechanical histories, resulting in a wide spectrum of mechanical properties among various microstructural constituents. More recently, carbon segregation at PAGBs was shown to significantly enhance resistance to hydrogen-induced intergranular fracture in hydrogen-charged low-carbon steels  [33] . However, a comprehensive investigation into the distribution of chemical elements and strain localization at PAGBs, as well as their effects on local damage initiation in lath-martensitic Q&T and Q&P steels, is still necessary.

Therefore, to address the impact of PAGBs and RA on localized deformation in lath-martensitic high-strength steels, this study employs a quantitative and statistical approach at the nanoscopic scale, while still encompassing a large field-of-view. A comprehensive comparative analysis is conducted on medium-carbon, low-alloyed Q&T and Q&P steels with identical chemical compositions. Atomic-scale investigations of carbon partitioning between RA and martensite, as well as carbon segregation at PAGBs, are carried out using atom probe tomography (APT). The study further quantitatively examines the influence of RA in mitigating strain localization and partitioning at PAGBs and packet boundaries, and its subsequent effect on local damage initiation using HR-DIC technique.

sections.heading: Mechanical testing and HR-DIC

Uninterrupted uniaxial tensile tests were conducted to capture the macroscopic mechanical behaviors. The Q&P steel exhibits a yield strength of 1196 MPa, an ultimate strength of 1447 MPa and an elongation of 40.0%, while the Q&T steel exhibits a yield strength of 1465 MPa, an ultimate strength of 1952 MPa and an elongation of 23.6% (Supplementary Fig. S1). sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs: The initial microstructures of as-received Q&P and Q&T steels characterized by EBSD are illustrated in  Fig. 1 .  Fig. 1 (a) and (b) show the band contrast (BC) superimposed with phase map, and BC superimposed with inverse pole figure (IPF) of Q&P steel, respectively. The reconstructed PAGB is highlighted by a thicker line compared to the block boundary. There is 12.0% volume fraction of RA in the Q&P steel estimated from EBSD, while the XRD data reveals 16.1% volume fraction of RA. This discrepancy may be attributed to the thin-film RA at the boundary which is beyond the resolution of EBSD, and the slight martensite transformation during mechanical polishing. Blocky RA grains are predominantly located at PAGBs and packet boundaries, while a few film RA grains are situated at block boundaries and embedded within neighboring packets (more details in Supplementary Fig. S3). Two distinct types of martensite are observed: coarse-lath martensite (CM) grains with large size and relatively equiaxed shape located at PAGBs, and fine-lath martensite (FM) grains that are uniformly distributed. It is known that some unstable retained austenite may transform into fresh martensite during the final stage of the Q&P treatment. However, in this study, the mechanically polished specimen was not etched to maintain a flat surface for HR-DIC speckle production, making it challenging to capture the extremely small fresh martensite through subsequent EBSD and BSE observations. Consequently, limited fresh martensite was treated as standard lath-martensite for simplicity.  Fig. 1 (c) depicts the stitched BSE micrograph superimposed with the block boundaries and PAGBs obtained from EBSD. The good alignment between the BSE micrograph and undistorted EBSD is confirmed. The inset highlights the sufficiently small and uniformly distributed DIC patterns.  Fig. 1 (d), (e), and (f) display the phase map, IPF, and stitched BSE micrograph of the Q&T steel, respectively. The Q&T steel exhibits a martensitic structure, comprising a few large CM grains and a more uniformly distributed lamellar FM grains. Within the large reconstructed prior austenite grain in the ROI, a large packet with parallel FM is observed, leading to a significant connection in morphology.

Fig. 2  presents quantitative insights into the atomic element distribution at various interfaces. APT tip-1 was positioned at the interface between RA and FM in the Q&P steel ( Fig. 2 (a)), with the microstructure of the thin foil characterized by STEM in  Fig. 2 (b). Both RA and FM exhibit a fine lamellar morphology with a thickness of approximately 150 nm. Numerous initial dislocations are observed in both the bulk and boundaries of RA and FM. The selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns, shown in the inset, reveal a KS-OR between RA and FM in the current Q&P steel.  Fig. 2 (e) and (f) display the carbon and manganese atom maps of tip-1, respectively. The 7 at. 
                            % 
                          iso-composition surfaces of carbon are highlighted in blue in  Fig. 2 (e). The bulk of RA exhibits a significantly higher carbon concentration compared to the bulk of FM, while manganese is homogeneously distributed in the bulk areas of both RA and FM. There is a notable segregation of carbon and manganese at the phase boundary (PB). In addition to the substantial high carbon islands concentrating at the PB, numerous high carbon islands appear in the bulk of RA. Furthermore, a few high carbon enrichment regions in FM, highlighted by white arrows, suggest the potential presence of lath interfaces within the FM. These areas of carbon enrichment could also be precursors to carbide formation. A profile representing the quantitatively heterogeneous element distribution at the PB is provided in  Fig. 2 (i). While aluminum and silicon are uniformly distributed throughout the Q&P steel, the coexistence of carbon and manganese enrichment at the PB is evident, with a much higher carbon concentration peak of 9.6 at. 
                            % 
                          compared to the manganese concentration peak of 4.8 at.

                         . On the other hand, APT tip-2 was positioned at the PAGB in the Q&T steel ( Fig. 2 (c)), with the microstructure of the thin foil characterized by STEM in  Fig. 2 (d). Both the IPF and TEM micrograph show the straight PAGB, which also serves as the interface between CM and FM in different prior austenite grains. The PAGB is notably thicker and longer than the other block boundaries. The FM grains exhibit a higher initial dislocation density compared to the CM (more details in Supplementary Fig. S4), with strongly deflected block boundaries and residual stress concentration. The SAED pattern at the PAGB confirms the presence of single BCC-martensite.  Fig. 2 (g) and (h) display the carbon and manganese atom maps of tip-2 at the PAGB in the Q&T steel, respectively. Intensive carbon segregation is observed at the PAGB, while there is no apparent manganese segregation. Similar to the carbon distribution in FM of the Q&P steel, the carbon enrichment regions in FM of the Q&T steel also form lath boundaries, as highlighted by the white arrows (more details in Supplementary Fig. S5). A profile showcasing the quantitative atomic element distribution at the PAGB in the cylinder region is presented in  Fig. 2 (j). Notable carbon enrichment is observed at the PAGB with a concentration peak of 11.5 at. 
                            % 
                         . Pronounced gradients are observed at both sides of the FM and CM interfaces, indicating a sharp carbon transfer and absorption behavior near PAGB. The thickness of the PAGB is estimated to be 10.2 nm, significantly thicker than that of the PB at 4.0 nm. The average carbon concentration in the bulk of CM is 1.19 at. 
                            % 
                         , whereas in the bulk of FM it is 1.88 at. 
                            % 
                         . However, aluminum, silicon, and manganese are uniformly distributed throughout.

The nanohardness measurements of Q&P and Q&T steels exhibit a diverse range of mechanical strength. As illustrated in  Fig. 3 (a), although the CM and RA display a similar nanohardness range in the Q&P steel, a greater fraction of RA exhibits higher nanohardness values. The FM demonstrates the highest nanohardness value, accompanied by the largest dispersion. In the Q&T steel as depicted in  Fig. 3 (b), the nanohardness distributions of FM and CM are similar to those of the Q&P steel, yet with notably higher values in the Q&T steel. The box-and-whisker plot in  Fig. 3 (c) distinctly delineates the nanohardness variations among the different microstructural constituents in both Q&P and Q&T steels. In the Q&P steel, the FM showcases the highest average nanohardness value of 7.8 GPa, whereas the RA exhibits a slightly higher average nanohardness value of 6.7 GPa compared to 6.4 GPa in the CM. Despite the differing average values in RA and CM, the non-outlier minimums calculated based on the interquartile range for the microstructural constituents remain similar. It is noteworthy that no evident martensitic transformation in RA following nanoindentation has been observed within the resolution of EBSD. In the Q&T steel, the FM and CM have average nanohardness values of 10.6 and 9.5 GPa respectively, markedly higher than all the constituents in the Q&P steel. Note that due to the smaller volume fractions of RA and CM, the validated indents within the bulk of CM and RA free from boundary influence, are significantly fewer than in FM, resulting in reduced scattering and non-normal distribution.

Fig. 4 (a), (b), and (c) depict the equivalent strain maps superimposed with block boundaries and PAGBs at average strain levels of 1.3%, 6.9%, and 13.0% in Q&P steel, respectively. In the early-stage of plastic deformation ( Fig. 4 (a)), strain localizations primarily occur at PAGBs (highlighted by red arrows), with a few also observed at specific packet (highlighted by white arrow). As the global strain increases ( Fig. 4 (b) and (c)), the number and intensity of strain localizations at PAGBs and preferred FM regions are enhanced. Pronounced strain partitioning among different constituents occurs simultaneously. Moreover, substantial slip activities are observed in CM, traversing through the embedded FM grains. The highly deformed PAGBs and their vicinities, along with the CM and surrounding FM, are interconnected, forming mesoscopic shear bands.  Fig. 4 (d), (e), and (f) illustrate the equivalent strain maps superimposed with block boundaries and PAGBs at average strain levels of 1.4%, 8.5%, and 16.0% in Q&T steel, respectively. Similarly, in the early-stage of plastic deformation ( Fig. 4 (d)), significant strain localizations occur at both PAGBs (highlighted by red arrows) and specific packets and boundaries (highlighted by white arrows). However, unlike the Q&P steel, the thin strain channels in Q&T steel exhibit a strong geometric orientation preference at 45 
                            ° 
                          to the loading direction. Moreover, the individual high strain spots are connected, leading to the early formation of mesoscopic shear bands. As the global strain increases ( Fig. 4 (e) and (f)), the phenomenon of strain localization and partitioning is intensified at the original deformation bands, without evident strain spreading to adjacent low-strain zones. Meanwhile, the CM undergoes significant deformation due to slip activities, with the region close to the PAGB exhibiting more deformation compared to the center of the prior austenite grain.

The statistical and quantitative comparison of global strain distribution between Q&P and Q&T steels is presented in  Fig. 5 . The strain distribution is analyzed using probability density (PD). In both materials, the concentration on low strain values indicates the onset of plastic deformation at the early-stage of straining. As global strain increases, the strain distributions exhibit a widening spectrum and an enhancement in the fraction of high strain values. Additionally, at all three comparable strain levels, Q&T steel shows a greater fraction of areas experiencing both significantly lower and higher deformation compared to Q&P steel, suggesting more pronounced strain localization and inhomogeneity.

sections.heading: Local strain partitioning
paragraphs:
To quantitatively investigate the strain partitioning and RA deformation in Q&P steel, strain profiles along different illustrative paths and corresponding microstructures are displayed in  Fig. 7 . The enlarged strain map is selected due to the comprehensive microstructure components including PAGB, FM, RA, CM, and representative multiple deformation mechanisms.  Fig. 7 (e) depicts a profile of strain evolution along path A, crossing PAGBs, martensite, and RA. Two distinct deformation behaviors are observed at PAGBs. The left PAGB exhibits limited strain on both sides despite the high induced strain level, resulting in significant strain gradients crossing the neighboring grains. In contrast, significant strain localization and partitioning occur at the right PAGB at the early-stage of deformation, with intensity increasing as the applied strain increases. At the block boundary within the same packet (distance of  
                            
                               0 
                               . 
                               25 
                               
                               μ 
                               m 
                            
                         ), a smooth strain distribution occurs until 6.9% global strain level, while pronounced strain localization and partitioning occur at 13.0% and 20.3% global strain levels. It is interesting to note that despite the RA grains being located close to the highly deformed PAGB, they do not exhibit notable deformation since they are embedded in a hard FM matrix. On the other hand, relatively homogeneous strain distribution and moderate strain localization are observed at the PAGB along path B as shown in  Fig. 7 (f), which is the interface between CM and RA. Almost no deformation is apparent in the bulk area of CM and RA, as well as the PAGB at the 0.5% and 1.3% global strain levels. However, significant slip deformation is activated based on the Schmid law in CM from the 6.9% global strain level, resulting in discrete high-strain thin channels. Meanwhile, the RA deforms simultaneously, most likely due to the slip deformation and martensite transformation. Note that a small FM grain is embedded inside the blocky RA grain, creating a local high-strength island, and therefore strain discontinuity. In the RA grain, a decreasing strain gradient from PAGB to the bulk suggests that slip and martensite transformation may initiate from the PAGB and then propagate to the bulk area. The strain evolution along path C representing deformation in CM and an embedded FM grains is shown in  Fig. 7 (g). At early-stage of loading, almost no deformation occurs in both CM and the embedded FM grain. However, at the 6.9% global strain level, CM and FM grains deform simultaneously with similar intensity, without evident strain partitioning occurring at the interfaces. As the global strain increases, the discrete slips in CM glide more significantly, resulting in an overall higher strain consumption in CM than in the embedded FM. Moreover, the slip transmission from CM into FM is more strongly hindered by the interfaces at high strain levels, resulting in an obvious strain partitioning. Finally, the strain evolution along path D representing deformation in different packets is shown in  Fig. 7 (h). A limited strain localization initially occurs at the packet boundary, while more obvious heterogeneous deformation is observed in the bulk of FM with multiple in-lath slip activities. With an increase in the global strain level, the strain concentration at the packet boundary is enhanced, while the strain localization becomes considerably severer in the bulk of FM due to the increment in number and intensity of in-lath slip activities. Moreover, among the packets with active in-lath slip, slip transmission from a FM grain to a RA grain (RA1) occurs as highlighted by the white arrow in  Fig. 7 (a) and (b).

Likewise, the heterogeneous strain distribution and localization in Q&T steel are quantitatively investigated, as shown in  Fig. 8 . Deforming behaviors at PAGBs, packet boundaries, and CM/FM interfaces are selected and enlarged from  Fig. 4 (f).  Fig. 8 (a) displays the equivalent strain map of a PAGB and neighboring FM grains, while  Fig. 8 (d) depicts the corresponding strain evolution along the microscopic path crossing the PAGB. At early-stage of deformation, substantial strain localization already occurs along the entire straight PAGB, with a preferred geometric orientation of 45 
                            ° 
                          to the loading direction. Meanwhile, moderate strain localizations also occur at the packet boundary. In the bulk of FM grains neighboring the PAGB, substantial in-lath slip deformation is activated simultaneously. As the global strain increases, significant strain partitioning is observed at both the PAGB and packet boundaries. In the prior austenite grain to the left of the PAGB, most of the area is occupied by packet 2 (in red) with an in-lath slip trace perpendicular to the PAGB, whereas only a thin layer of packet 4 (in green) exists parallel to the PAGB, with a high Schmid factor for the in-lath slip system. Consequently, limited strain localizations occur at the block boundaries in packet 2, while significant strain is accommodated by substantial in-lath slip activities in packet 4. On the other hand, in the prior austenite grain to the right of the PAGB, packets 2 and 4 exhibit similar geometric orientations and mechanical responses, such as being parallel to the PAGB, having similar in-lath slip traces and Schmid factors. However, FM grains in packet 4 possess a greater longitudinal length and a stronger network compared to packet 2, leading to substantial in-lath slip deformation in packet 4 and significant strain partitioning at the packet boundary.  Fig. 8 (b) depicts an equivalent strain map focusing on a packet boundary far from the PAGB, with the corresponding strain evolution across the packet boundary shown in  Fig. 8 (e). The packet boundary also exhibits a 45 
                            ° 
                          orientation to the loading direction, with the longitudinal direction and in-lath slip trace of packet 2 being parallel, but packet 4 being perpendicular. Pronounced strain partitioning occurs at the packet boundary, where packet 4 deforms minimally despite the high imposed global strain, while considerable in-lath slip systems are activated in packet 2 even at the early-stage of deformation. This is due to the high in-lath Schmid factor and the massive network along the longitudinal direction. Finally, the deformation in a CM grain and an embedded FM grain is displayed in  Fig. 8 (c), with the strain evolution at the CM/FM interface shown in  Fig. 8 (f). The microscopic path in the CM grain follows a slip trace with the highest Schmid factor for the

                                  110

                                  〈 
                                  111 
                                  〉 
                               
                            
                          slip system. These two grains are two blocks, belonging to the same packet but having different crystal orientations. At the early-stage of deformation, almost no strain is accommodated by the CM and the embedded FM grains. However, at an 8.5% average strain level, slip deformation based on Schmid law occurs in the CM, and in-lath slip deformation (highlighted by the yellow arrow) in the FM is activated, with slight strain partitioning taking place at the CM/FM interface. As the global strain increases, slip intensity is enhanced, and multiple slip systems (but not the in-lath slip system) are activated in the CM. Meanwhile, in the FM, along with the enhancement of in-lath slip activity, strain transmission (highlighted by the white arrow) from the CM matrix into the FM grain occurs. This slip transmission provides an additional way for strain accommodation and also prohibits further strain partitioning at the CM/FM interface.

sections.heading: Fracture behavior
paragraphs: Upon reaching a heavily deformed state in Q&P and Q&T steels, surface-local damages such as micro voids and steps form and grow, which are characterized in detail in  Fig. 9 .  Fig. 9 (a) shows the SEM micrograph in the ROI of Q&P steel at a 20.3% average strain level, with the corresponding equivalent strain map inset. The prominent surface voids and steps are predominantly located at PAGBs, as highlighted and enlarged in  Fig. 9 (A1), (A2), (A3), and (A4) plots. The formation of local damages typically begins with the development of micro voids at PAGBs (A3 and A4), followed by the coalescence and the creation of severe surface steps along the PAGB (A2), eventually propagating over the surrounding regions (A1). Throughout the process of local damage formation and propagation in Q&P steel, the nucleation and growth of micro voids play a crucial role in local strain accommodation, consistent with the fractography observations shown in Supplementary Fig. S6.  Fig. 9 (b) presents the heavy-deformation state in the ROI of Q&T steel at a 24.5% average strain level, with examples of local damages highlighted and enlarged in  Fig. 9 (B1), (B2), and (B3) plots. At a comparable global deformation state, Q&T steel exhibits much more severe surface damages with higher quantity and intensity compared to Q&P steel. In addition to the presence of surface steps at PAGBs (B1 and B2), mesoscopic steps form along packet boundaries, where substantial strain localization and partitioning phenomena occur. Moreover, limited micro voids are nucleated even at heavily deformed sites in Q&T steel, while significant shear bands form parallel or perpendicular to each other, resulting in strong local interaction and discrepancy.

sections.heading: Discussions
paragraphs: Quantitative and statistical analyses have been conducted through nanoscopic HR-DIC strain probing experiments and comprehensive microstructural characterizations in Q&P and Q&T steels. Heterogeneous elemental distribution and significant strain partitioning are observed among different microstructural constituents and at preferred boundaries. Under heavily applied loading conditions, local damage precursors initiate and propagate along specific boundaries. However, bridging the understanding gap between atomic element distribution, nanoscopic mechanical response, and microscopic local damage still presents a challenge. To address this gap, in the following sections, the roles of retained austenite in terms of chemical composition effect and mechanical response effect (Section  4.1 ), the interface plasticity (Section  4.2 ), and the strain localization and damage initiation (Section  4.3 ) will be discussed.

sections.heading: Roles of retained austenite
paragraphs: The equivalent strain distributions of martensite (M) and RA in Q&P steel are illustrated in  Fig. 10 (a). It should be noted that the strain in RA accounts for both martensite transformation and subsequent slip deformation. Despite the increase in applied strain, the distribution of martensite and RA remains unchanged, with a higher fraction of highly deformed regions (above 80%) and a lower fraction of less deformed regions (below 20%) in RA compared to martensite. In contrast, the median strain portions of martensite and RA overlap, indicating an overall consistent deformation intensity.  Fig. 10 (b) provides a more quantitative insight into the evolution of strain distribution in martensite and RA, along with the evolution of RA volume fraction as the applied strain increases. The symbols represent the average equivalent strain values, while the vertical lines represent the standard deviations. The martensite transformation proceeds smoothly as the applied strain increases, with 3.9% volume fraction of RA remaining untransformed despite the high imposed strain. Generally, both martensite and RA equally accommodate the applied strain due to their similar average strain values at all global strain levels. However, RA exhibits a much more pronounced strain inhomogeneity, which becomes more pronounced as the applied strain increases, suggesting a wide spectrum of RA stability.

In addition to the carbon composition, the crystallographic orientation, grain size and local stain state of the surrounding constituent are critical factors governing the mechanical stability of RA  [16,22,50,51] . High Schmid factor RA grains were reported to undergo either severe crystal rotation  [52,53] , or martensite transformation  [54] . Large blocky RA was reported to possess a lower mechanical stability than thin RA  [51,55] . However, these neighborhood-independent factors alone do not fully explain the heterogeneous deformation behavior of RA in current Q&P steel, as depicted in  Fig. 6 . The observed neighboring effect, influenced by the local strain state of surrounding constituents governing RA deformation, aligns with findings in various steels  [22,23,29,56] . In a martensitic structural Q&P steel, moderate strain localization at PAGBs, packet, and block boundaries was noted, albeit without deeper exploration of RA contribution  [56] . In the current medium-carbon Q&P steel with a lath-martensitic structure, RA grains proximate to highly deformed PAGBs undergo severer deformation compared to grains within the hard FM matrix. Moreover, according to the global strain evolution illustrated in  Fig. 4 (a), (b), and (c), mesoscopic shear bands inclined 45 
                            ° 
                          to the loading direction have formed due to the connections of highly deformed PAGBs and their vicinities, as well as the CM and surrounding FM grains as the applied strain increases. Due to the stable interface between RA and martensite, the strain from the martensite matrix spreads into the RA along the shear band, as highlighted by a dashed line circle in  Fig. 6 (b) and demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S7. Note that the intensity of strain localization along the shear bands in Q&P steel is much lower than in Q&T steel. This RA deformation, based on the preferred spatial alignment relative to the loading direction, was also pointed out in the Ref.  [24] . Meanwhile, small RA grains embedded in significantly activated in-lath slip packets also severely deform (for example, RA1 grain in  Fig. 6 (b)), due to the slip transmission as shown in  Fig. 7 (a). This can be attributed to the fact that one  
                            
                               { 
                               111 
                               } 
                            
                          slip plane in RA is parallel to the interfacial habit plane  [57] . This is complemented by another strain spreading phenomenon as illustrated in  Fig. 7 (f), where the deformation is initiated within the blocky RA island and then propagates into the FM lath. Therefore, the synergistic effect of strain spreading arisen from the complex RA and martensite interactions promotes significant strain accommodation at strain localization sites, leading to a reduce of strain partitioning intensity.

In summary, although RA overall accommodates the imposed strain similarly to martensite and some RA grains remain untransformed, its presence serves multiple important functions. RA not only absorbs carbon, maintaining low strength and high deformability, but also uniformly distributes and induces stable interfaces. The gradually released TRIP effect primarily occurs at strain localization and partitioning boundaries, particularly at PAGBs, effectively mitigating local strain incompatibilities.

sections.heading: Interface plasticity
paragraphs: The strain distribution and evolution of all boundaries, PAGB, and bulk in Q&P and Q&T steels are depicted in  Fig. 10 (c), (d), (e) and (f). All boundaries defined here include block boundaries, packet boundaries and PAGBs as detected and reconstructed based on EBSD results as shown in  Fig. 1 . While the block boundaries and PAGBs observed in TEM and APT are on the order of tens of nanometers, the deformation probed by HR-DIC still reveals a relatively wider strain spreading, with strong interaction along the boundary vicinities. Therefore, the thickness of all boundaries is set to be 40 pixels in the HR-DIC strain map. The bulk here then refers to the area in the ROI except for all boundaries. A more clear illustration is provided in Supplementary Fig. S8. The volume fraction of all boundaries, bulk and PAGB in the ROI of Q&P steel are 49.9%, 50.1% and 12.5%, respectively, while those of Q&T steel are 50.8%, 49.2% and 5.0%, respectively. In Q&P steel, the distributions of all boundaries and bulk are very close, while the PAGB exhibits a similar distribution but with higher strain values covering the entire range of deformation magnitudes. The difference between the PAGB and all boundaries/bulk distributions increases as the applied strain increases. The average normalized equivalent strain values indicate that strain concentration occurs at the PAGB from the early-stage of deformation, with higher intensity as the global strain increases. Meanwhile, the bulk accommodates more strain compared to all boundaries, with the ability to consume strain becoming stronger with increasingly severe loading. Unlike the smooth increase in strain localization behavior in Q&P steel, Q&T steel displays substantial strain localization at the PAGB from a low global strain level, continuing this tendency into severe deformation stages. As the global strain increases, the distribution of the bulk in Q&T steel shifts from being closer to all boundaries to being closer to the PAGB, resulting in a stronger increase in the average value and inhomogeneity.

The quantitative assessment of atomic element distribution at the PAGB in Q&T steel is investigated using APT, as depicted in  Fig. 2 (j). Notable carbon segregation occurs, aligning with observations in various steel studies  [58,59] . While no APT characterization was performed at the PAGB in Q&P steel in this study, it is plausible to speculate that the PAGB in Q&P steel exhibits less intensive carbon segregation due to the carbon absorption in RA and the carbon redistribution pathway in lath martensite  [22,60] . Hence, one hypothesis regarding the pronounced strain localization observed at the PAGBs during microscopic yielding is that the presence of numerous high carbon islands induces significant lattice distortion and the formation of large vacancies, thereby reducing yielding resistance compared to other microstructural constituents. The higher intensity of carbon segregation in Q&T steel facilitates easier onset of deformation at PAGBs, resulting in more significant strain localization and a greater tendency to persist compared to Q&P steel. However, further evidence, such as detailed TEM observations on atomic movement and misalignment, is required to validate this theory. An in-depth investigation into the locations of severely deformed PAGBs during straining reveals distinct behavior between the Q&P and Q&T steels. In Q&P steel, the PAGBs adjacent to large clusters of FM grains, lacking a packet with a longitudinal direction parallel to boundaries and a feasible in-lath slip system, primarily undergo deformation. Conversely, in Q&T steel, the PAGBs inclined at a 45 
                            ° 
                          angle to the loading direction, with at least one side exhibiting a packet with a longitudinal direction parallel to boundaries and a feasible in-lath slip system, are mainly subjected to deformation. This variation in mechanical response is likely attributed to the differences in microstructural constituents and morphology resulting from distinct heat treatment processes.

The packet boundaries in both Q&P and Q&T steels experience notable strain localization as depicted in  Figs. 7 and 8 . However, Q&T steel exhibits a significantly higher occurrence and intensity of this phenomenon. The packet boundary exhibits asymmetry, with one side of the packet laths lying parallel to the boundary, while the other side ends with a short edge  [30] . This microscopic morphology is more pronounced in Q&T steel than in Q&P steel due to the absence of RA as a consequence of thorough quenching process. Therefore, in Q&T steel, in-lath slip deformation is predominantly activated in the large packets parallel to the boundary and aligning at a 45 
                            ° 
                          angle to the loading direction, thereby strongly impeding the transfer of plastic deformation  [61] . This leads to a more pronounced strain partitioning at the packet boundary in Q&T steel compared to Q&P steel. The block boundary also exhibits significantly heterogeneous deformation in both Q&P and Q&T steels. When the in-lath slip system within the large packet is not strongly activated, or when the lath FM remains distant from highly deformed CM, there is limited interface plasticity at the block boundary. However, when the block boundary is preferentially oriented to the local stress condition, the coexistence of boundary sliding and crystallographic slip substantially promotes the interface plasticity  [62] . Moreover, according to the APT carbon map reconstruction in Q&P and Q&T steels as shown in  Fig. 2 (e) and (g), and Supplementary Fig. S5, local high carbon planes appeared in the bulk of FM grains, which were also observed in other steel and characterized to be fine lath boundaries  [63] . It was reported that the dislocation motion was hindered by the lath boundaries, and upon reaching a critical stress, a high density of dislocations transferred in to the adjacent lath region  [64] . Thus, these fine lath boundaries beyond the EBSD resolution, may result in considerable strain accommodation capacity in the bulk area defined above.

sections.heading: Strain localization and damage initiation
paragraphs: In the polycrystalline materials, it is commonly held that damage nucleation occurs in locations of substantial strain concentration  [65] . Recent studies utilizing the HR-DIC technique in various steels, have found that local damage, including surface steps and micro voids, predominantly nucleated at strain partitioning boundaries  [21,30,32,66] . Moreover, a three-dimensional EBSD characterization in lath-martensitic steel clearly revealed that intergranular cracks propagated along the PAGBs, with large martensite variants and low-angle misorientation boundaries enhancing stress concentration accommodation and resulting in crack-tip blunting  [67] . Consistently, the major surface steps and micro voids are predominantly situated at the PAGBs in current Q&P steel, where pronounced strain localization and partitioning occur. In contrast, in Q&T steel, severe surface steps are also observed at heavily deformed packet boundaries in addition to the PAGBs. As discussed in Sections  4.1 and 4.2 , RA not only absorbs carbon but also provides a considerable TRIP effect. Therefore, although the Q&P steel also experiences strain localization and partitioning phenomena, the intensity is much lower compared to the Q&T steel, resulting in local damage primarily concentrating on the relatively embrittled PAGBs. Moreover, the fractography detected by SEM and micro X-ray computed tomography also reveals a more ductile fracture behavior of Q&P steel compared to the Q&T steel (Supplementary Fig. S6).

The local microstructural strain path, often divergent from the applied macroscopic strain path due to local plastic anisotropy, plays an important role in influencing the initiation of local damage  [23,68] . Studies on dual-phase steel have indicated that strain bands along the maximum shear direction predominantly deform under uniaxial tension (UAT), while those perpendicular to the loading direction exhibit behavior akin to plane strain tension (PST)  [68] . In sheet metal forming, PST has been observed to exhibit the least susceptibility to plastic instability and fracture, as the strain is primarily accommodated through thickness reduction  [23] . Therefore, the local microstructural configurations of PST strain paths appear to be potential sites of early failure origins.  Fig. 11 (a) and (b) illustrate the microstructural strain paths associated with strain localization incidents in microscopic damage areas and CM grains of Q&P and Q&T steels, respectively. The strain localization incidents in microscopic damage areas were selected from the top 10% most strained subsets at the last loading interruption. sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In present work, the role of prior austenite grain boundary (PAGB) and retained austenite (RA) on the heterogeneous chemical element distribution and mechanical response has been comprehensively investigated through nanoscopic atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution digital image correlation (HR-DIC) over a mesoscopic field-of-view. A comparison study between a quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steel and a quenching and tempering (Q&T) steel is performed. Precise alignment between HR-DIC strain map and distortion-corrected EBSD map provides quantitative and statistic insights into the strain localization and partitioning at multiple sites, especially the interface plasticity. Consequently, the precursors of local damage are clearly characterized and linked to the microstructural strain states. The main results are summarized as follows:

1. 
                            APT measurements quantitatively illustrate the coexistence of carbon and manganese segregation at the interface between RA and martensite, attributed to carbon partitioning from martensite to RA, as well as significant carbon segregation at the PAGB. Nanohardness measurements of various microstructural constituents align with the observed chemical element distribution. Specifically, fine-lath martensite exhibits the highest nanohardness value, while the stabilized RA demonstrates nanohardness comparable to that of the coarse-lath martensite on average. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            Quantitative and statistical analysis of strain evolution reveals significant strain localization and partitioning behavior, particularly at the interface plasticity sites such as PAGB, packet boundary, and block boundary. Both Q&P and Q&T steels exhibit pronounced strain localization at PAGB due to carbon segregation. In Q&P steel, the PAGBs adjacent to large clusters of FM grains, lacking a packet with longitudinal direction parallel to boundaries and a feasible in-lath slip system, primarily undergo deformation. On the other hand, in Q&T steel, the PAGBs inclined at a 45 
                                  ° 
                                angle to the loading direction, with at least one side exhibiting a packet with longitudinal direction parallel to boundaries and a feasible in-lath slip system, are mainly subjected to deformation. This variation in mechanical response is attributed to the differences in microstructural constituents and morphology resulting from distinct heat treatment processes. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The yielding of RA exhibits a strong neighborhood-dependent phenomenon. RA plays a crucial role by absorbing carbon, and forming stable interfaces that prevent the development of large packets prone to in-lath slip transmission. The TRIP effect, which is gradually activated, primarily takes place at strain localization and partitioning boundaries, especially at PAGBs, thereby reducing local strain incompatibilities. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The major surface steps and micro voids are predominantly situated at the PAGBs, where pronounced strain localization and partitioning occur. In Q&P steel, significant microstructural strain paths align closely with plane strain tension at heavily deformed states, promoting micro voids nucleation and strain accommodation. Conversely, in Q&T steel, the majority of microstructural strain paths remain aligned with uniaxial tension, resulting in significant shear bands formation at preferentially oriented boundaries.
